items.title: Anthropic files public S-1 with the SEC for proposed IPO on Nasdaq — ticker 'ANT', H1 2026 revenue $16.3B (≈15× YoY), two customers = 25% of revenue, $80.7B non-cash loss, LTBT codified as Class T directors with Founder-LLC Class F super-voting share; Reuters now reports investor pushback has pulled valuation discussion from ~$2T down to ~$1.5T
items.summary: Anthropic announced on October 26, 2026 that it has filed a Form S-1 registration statement with the SEC for a proposed initial public offering of Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker 'ANT'. The public filing is now live on EDGAR (anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) alongside the Class F exhibit (exhibit33-sx1.htm). Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and Citi are the banks working with Anthropic on the offering per secondary reporting; the Anthropic announcement itself lists Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters. Share count and price range are not yet set. The draft S-1 — reviewed by the Wall Street Journal and summarized by multiple outlets — reports H1 2026 revenue of about $16.3B (Q1 ≈ $4.73B, Q2 ≈ $11.5B), up from about $1.1B in H1 2025 — roughly a 15× year-over-year jump. Reported H1 2026 net loss is $80.7B, overwhelmingly a non-cash charge tied to re-valuation of convertible financing instruments as the company's implied valuation climbed; adjusted operating income is reported positive for the quarter per Bloomberg. Two unnamed customers accounted for about 25% of H1 revenue; Amazon and Google marketplaces together generated roughly 47% of 2025 revenue, highlighting significant channel concentration. Cited compute commitments range from $518B (one report) to more than $600B, with up to $750B when deals under negotiation are included. The S-1 formalizes a three-class share structure: Class A (public), Class T (held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust — no economic rights; the trust elects and removes the Class T directors, who will constitute a majority of the board), and a single share of Class F common stock issued to the Founder LLC immediately prior to the offering, entitled to 50.1% of total voting power on certain matters. The Class F exhibit specifies that the holder can split its vote at its discretion up to that total voting power; the Founder LLC itself is controlled by majority vote of the seven co-founders. Anthropic will remain a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation. New overnight: Reuters-sourced reporting from Anthropic's SF investor day indicates that attendees are discussing a ~$1.5T IPO valuation for the November share sale, down from the roughly $2T previously expected, tied to Q3 revenue growth of 45% to $16.8B — slower sequentially than Q2's near-doubling. Michael Burry has publicly questioned whether Anthropic and SpaceX deserve trillion-dollar public valuations. Secondary reporting also flags three new near-term risk factors: cheaper Chinese open-weight competition, tensions with the Trump administration, and backlash against US data center construction.
items.why_it_matters: This is the single most consequential governance and financial event in Anthropic's history, and it closes the loop on three stories the agent has been tracking across the past week: the Stubbs appointment to the LTBT (Oct 21, in yesterday's am file), the Public Benefit Fund (Oct 18), and now the S-1 itself. The three items are not independent — they are the sequence of pre-IPO moves that collectively lock in the governance structure Anthropic plans to carry into public markets. What the S-1 reveals that was not previously public: (1) the LTBT is codified as the elector of a majority of the board via Class T stock — not an advisory committee but a legally binding mechanism; (2) the Founder LLC gets 50.1% voting power on certain matters via a single Class F share — the SpaceX / Snap / Google founder-control playbook, with an explicit twist that the founder super-vote and the LTBT board-election power coexist, so the trust can still pick the directors even while founders hold voting control on specified matters; the Class F exhibit now on EDGAR adds that the holder can split its vote at discretion up to the share's full voting power, and the Founder LLC itself is run by majority vote of the seven co-founders — a feature that means no single founder can unilaterally wield the super-vote; (3) the PBC status is preserved rather than converted, which means fiduciary duty requires balancing shareholder pecuniary interests, the interests of those materially affected by the company, and the stated public benefit purpose. The financials are the other half of the story: ≈15× YoY revenue growth is at a scale that very few operating companies have achieved at this valuation level, but customer concentration (two customers = 25% of H1 revenue, Amazon + Google marketplaces = 47% of 2025 revenue) is the specific risk factor every reader of the eventual public S-1 will underline. The $80.7B 'loss' is a non-cash accounting artifact of the convertible financing round, not a cash burn number — distinguishing the two is going to be the central interpretive battle in press coverage over the next three weeks. The compute commitments ($518B–$600B+, up to $750B including deals in negotiation) are the number that matters for understanding why the company needs public-market capital: Anthropic is pre-committing to compute spend at a scale that no amount of private financing can plausibly cover, which is itself the operational reason for the IPO. New overnight: the valuation story has shifted from aspirational ($2T target per secondary coverage) to contested ($1.5T floor per Reuters' investor-day reporting, tied to a Q3 growth slowdown to 45% QoQ at $16.8B revenue — which also reconciles the earlier 'disputed $16.8B Q3-only' figure as actually a Q3 total, not an alternative H1 number). The reconciliation matters because it means investors are now pricing against three sequential data points — H1 of $16.3B, Q3 of $16.8B, and an implied Q4 ramp — rather than a single H1 datum. Michael Burry's public skepticism is the first well-known short-biased investor voice publicly questioning the valuation; it will show up in Chancery-litigation briefing and in sell-side analyst notes within weeks. For Gabe, the direct relevance is twofold: (1) the SKILL.md format he interacts with every day inside Claude Code is now a product of a company that is about to be scrutinized by the SEC, equity analysts, and shareholders — the model-safety-vs-shareholder-return tension is no longer theoretical, it is a Delaware fiduciary-duty question embedded in a PBC charter he can go read on EDGAR; (2) the LTBT item in yesterday's am file was effectively the pre-game of this filing, so the governance-structure items the agent has been surfacing this week stack together into a complete picture rather than three separate curiosities. The honest caveats: (a) press figures do not all agree — H1 revenue cited ranges from $16.3B to a $16.8B figure that now looks like a Q3 standalone number from Reuters' investor-day reporting; compute commitments span $518B–$750B depending on which deals are counted; valuation targets ($1.5T–$2T) are from secondary reporting, not the filing itself; (b) the Delaware PBC fiduciary-duty structure is a plausible target for post-IPO shareholder litigation, and no company at Anthropic's scale has yet had its PBC commitments tested in Chancery Court; (c) the Class F super-vote has a specified set of matters it applies to — the exact perimeter of that set, as written in the filing, is the piece worth reading in the full text now that it is on EDGAR; (d) one Chinese-language cite in secondary coverage described the structure as 'Class B / Class T', which conflicts with the S-1's own 'Class A / Class T / Class F' naming, so trust the filing over the aggregator write-ups. The piece to watch over the next three weeks: pricing. Any pricing above the Series H's $965B is a public-market endorsement of the trust/founder-share governance structure; pricing below is the first market pushback on a PBC's ability to carry mission commitments through public listing — the exact test the governance-focused readers have been waiting for since Anthropic incorporated as a PBC.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 open weights now pointing to October 31 per Hugging Face listing — 1.05T total / 49B active MoE, 1M context, custom license (not Apache 2.0 like Large 3); Mistral docs still list weights + license as 'Coming soon'
items.summary: Mistral AI opened a public preview of Mistral Large 4 on October 6, 2026 with the full open-weights release committed to 'end of October'. Yesterday's digest cited Forklog's October 27 date; overnight searches now show the Hugging Face listing for 'Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B' pinning the ETA to October 31, 2026 — three outlets (aiweekly.co, Online Tech Tips, Hugging Face itself) line up on the Oct 31 target, so Oct 27 appears to have been a single-outlet mis-read of 'end of October'. The HF listing describes the model verbatim as 'a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal model'. The model's documentation lists approximately 1.05 trillion total parameters with around 49 billion active per query under a mixture-of-experts arrangement, plus a separate 1.6 billion-parameter vision encoder; the HF repo name suffix 'A52B' is the first public indication the active-parameter count could be 52B rather than 49B, which would reconcile a secondary-source discrepancy flagged yesterday. Mistral's docs quote a 1 million token context window; third-party tracker Vals AI's listing still shows 512k, so the real deployed context is worth confirming on release. Current preview access is a hosted API through Mistral Studio. The open-weights checkpoint will ship under a custom license — a departure from Large 3's Apache 2.0 — and Mistral's docs currently list both the weights and the license as 'Coming soon', meaning the license text itself has not been published yet. Early access is gated to developers, cybersecurity specialists, and government organizations; a separate private API with reduced moderation is reportedly available to 'privileged' partners including cybersecurity firms and state authorities. The model is too large to run on consumer hardware. Benchmark figures so far come from Mistral and are preliminary; Vals AI's independent Vals Index ranks Mistral Large 4 at #32 of 44 models with a 48.05% score.
items.why_it_matters: Mistral is the largest European lab still releasing open-weight frontier models at a competitive scale, and Large 4 is the piece of the Oct 2026 open-weights race that has been publicly committed to but not yet shipped. New overnight: the release target has firmed up as October 31 rather than October 27 (the Hugging Face listing for Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B now pins the ETA to Oct 31, and multiple outlets confirm — Forklog's Oct 27 cite now looks like a single-outlet mis-read of 'end of October'), so the Tier-1 moment for this story is Friday, not Tuesday. Three specifics still worth tracking before the weights land: (1) the custom-license departure from Apache 2.0 is the material story — Large 3 was broadly reusable under permissive terms, and a custom license on a trillion-parameter MoE will meaningfully shape who can self-host, redistribute, or build commercial products on top; critically, Mistral's docs still list the license as 'Coming soon' three days before release, so the license text is itself unreleased news; (2) the 1M vs 512k context discrepancy between Mistral's own docs and Vals AI's listing is the kind of fact that the weights release will settle definitively, so the config.json in the HuggingFace drop is the thing to read on arrival; (3) the private-API-with-reduced-moderation channel reportedly offered to cybersecurity firms and state authorities is a two-track safeguards story — relaxed safeguards for government and cybersec reads similar to Anthropic's LSVP tier for life-sciences orgs, but the perimeter is wider (not just one domain) and the licensing arrangement less visible, so the governance watchers will be comparing those two tiering programs directly. One further overnight nuance: the Hugging Face repo name suffix 'A52B' is the first public hint the active-parameter count could be 52B rather than the 49B figure in most secondary coverage, which would reconcile the discrepancy flagged in yesterday's digest — the config.json on Friday will settle this definitively. For Gabe: he does not need to run a 1T-parameter MoE locally — nobody with normal hardware does, and the HF-page coverage now confirms it 'is too large to run on a desktop or laptop' — but the arrival of a non-Apache-licensed trillion-parameter checkpoint on Hugging Face still matters because it fixes the ceiling for what a European open-weight release looks like under current competitive pressure, and because the smaller Mistral derivatives (if any ship this cycle) will be the ones that could run on consumer-grade hardware or appear quickly in Ollama. The honest caveats: (a) the Oct 31 date is now the plurality cite but Mistral itself only commits to 'end of October'; (b) all current benchmarks are Mistral-run and preliminary, and the Vals Index placement at #32/44 is strikingly weak for a trillion-parameter model, so independent evaluations after the weights land are the thing to watch; (c) the 49B vs 52B active-parameter discrepancy is small but matters for inference-cost math, since active-params × context dominates throughput costs on MoE serving — the HF repo-name 'A52B' points to 52B but is not yet confirmed by Mistral's docs. The piece to watch Friday: whether the custom license is permissive enough for commercial fine-tuning and redistribution, or whether it introduces the kind of 'you can download but not actually use at scale' constraint that gated Llama 2's early days — that distinction will decide whether Large 4 becomes the European open-weights ecosystem's anchor model or a technically-impressive but practically-constrained reference release.
